evidence: src/business/core/Event.ts: `@Entity()` on `export class Event` marks the domain class as a TypeORM table, which is persistence (infrastructure) work.
src/business/core/Event.ts: `@Column()` on the `id` property defines how the field is stored in the database, which is persistence (infrastructure) work.
src/business/core/Event.ts: `remaining()` and `sell()` (which throws SoldOut) are domain logic and fit the business layer.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/business/core/Event.ts is in the business layer, which is a domain layer. Most of the file is domain logic. remaining() works out capacity minus seats sold. sell() enforces the sold-out rule and works out the price. Both belong in a domain layer. The problem is that the class also maps itself to the database. The @Entity() decorator on the class and the @Column() decorator on the id field tell TypeORM how to store Event. That is persistence (infrastructure) work, and it now sits inside a domain entity. The import direction to 'typeorm' is checked by other tools and is not part of this review. The decorators are the issue: they give the domain class an ORM-mapping job that belongs in the persistence layer, for example a separate TypeORM schema or entity in src/persistence that maps to and from the domain Event.

violations.message: The domain entity Event maps itself to the database. The @Entity() decorator on the class and @Column() on the id field are TypeORM persistence mapping, which belongs in the persistence (infrastructure) layer, not the business (domain) layer.
